title: Lists, sets, maps, iterators, and choosing the correct collection
objectives: Define Apex List, Set, and Map using the Collections guide meanings.
Choose a list, set, or map from a signal such as order, uniqueness, or key lookup.
Walk a collection with for-each or an Iterator (hasNext/next) without inventing item-count limits.
Explain that collection size is heap-limited, not a fixed item cap.
diagnostic_question: You have duplicate LAB_ Account Ids from two queries, you must keep first-seen order for a UI, and you must later find a Case by AccountId. Which collections do you allocate, what do you iterate, and what do you refuse to put in a loop?
definition: Apex collections are lists, sets, or maps. A list is ordered and index-addressable. A set is unordered and unique. A map stores unique keys to values. There is no fixed item-count cap; heap size is the limit. Iterators traverse items with hasNext and next. ([Collections](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_collections.htm); [Lists](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_collections_lists.htm); [Custom Iterators](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_iterable.htm))
why_it_matters: The interview question is almost always 'why a Map of Id to Account instead of a list in a loop'. Wrong collection choice causes duplicate Ids, lost order, or SOQL in a loop. Saying 'a list can hold only 200 items' is a common invented limit.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a parcel sorting hub. A list is the numbered conveyor slots—order matters, duplicates can sit in two slots. A set is the unique-tracking scanner: the same barcode cannot occupy two unique bins. A map is the wall of cubbies: each barcode key opens exactly one cubby of contents. An iterator is the night walker who asks 'is there a next parcel?' and then takes it. The hub is not limited to a magic 200 parcels; the constraint is how much you can pile before the floor (heap) gives way.
deeper_explanation: Collections are lists, sets, or maps. Elements and keys can be primitives, sObjects, user-defined types, or nested collections. Apex is statically typed: you declare the type parameters. ([Collections](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_collections.htm))

A list is ordered; elements are distinguished by indices. Lists may nest up to seven inner collection levels (eight overall). Uninitialized lists are null until you assign a literal or new List<T>(). Array notation works for one-dimensional lists. ([Lists](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_collections_lists.htm))

A set does not contain duplicates and is unordered. A map is unique keys to a single value each. Sets and maps are the usual tools for Id uniqueness and Id-to-record lookup before a second query. Decimal keys with different scales can hash differently—Needs verification in your scenario; the primitives guide warns about Decimal in sets/maps.

An iterator traverses a collection. The Iterator interface requires hasNext and next, declared public or global. Iterable.iterator() returns that iterator. Custom iterators appear in Batchable start methods. A for-each loop is the everyday iterator. ([Custom Iterators](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_iterable.htm); [Loops](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_loops.htm))

mental_model.analogy: Parcel sorting hub: numbered conveyor (list), unique-tracking scanner (set), barcode cubbies (map), night walker asking hasNext (iterator).
useful_mapping: list → numbered conveyor slots; order and index matter
set → unique barcode scan; duplicates bounce
map → cubby wall; one key, one value
for-each → the everyday walker you do not write by hand
heap → floor load limit, not a 200-parcel myth
Id key → the barcode you should have queried once
nested list → a pallet of totes, up to documented nesting
where_it_breaks: Apex sets are unordered; a physical scanner tray might still look ordered.
sObject uniqueness in a set uses equality rules you must not invent—use Id sets when unsure.
The 200 figure people remember is a trigger batch size / for-loop batch size neighbor, not a collection item cap.
The analogy does not encode SOQL row limits.

teach_back_prompt: Using the sorting hub, explain when you choose a list, a set, or a map, how an iterator walks, and why 'max 200 items' is the wrong limit. Then name where the hub analogy breaks.

review_schedule.prompt: Define list, set, map, and iterator in one sentence each.
Given duplicate Ids plus a later lookup, pick set then map and say why not only a list.
Write for (Id i : idSet) and contrast it with a custom Iterator.
What limits a collection: heap versus invented item caps versus SOQL rows?
Two-minute interview: choose the correct collection with one bulkification example.

claims.claim: Collections in Apex can be lists, sets, or maps. There is no limit on the number of items a collection can hold; there is a general limit on heap size.
claims.validation: Collections page note on item count versus heap.

claims.claim: A list is an ordered collection whose elements are distinguished by indices. Lists can nest collections up to seven inner levels (eight overall) and are initialized to null until assigned.
A set is an unordered collection without duplicates. A map is unique keys to a single value. Keys and values can be primitives, sObjects, user-defined types, or collections.
An iterator traverses a collection via hasNext and next (public or global). Iterable.iterator() returns that iterator. for (variable : array_or_set) is the standard loop walk.

changed_in_release: Collection definitions are stable in Summer '26 (API 67.0). Reverify heap-size numbers on the governors page if an interview asks for a figure; this lesson does not invent one.
unresolved_uncertainty: Exact sObject equality in a Set<sObject> without Ids should be confirmed on current Set documentation before claiming field-based uniqueness.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: List keeps order and index. Set keeps unique values. Map looks up by key. Iterate with for-each or hasNext/next. Size is heap-bound, not a 200-item cap. Maps of Id prevent query-in-loop.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I gather Ids into a Set to drop duplicates, query once, and put results in a Map<Id, sObject> so the record loop uses get. I use a List when the UI or DML order matters. I do not invent a 200-item collection limit—the Collections page says heap is the constraint. I mention custom Iterator only when Batchable start or external paging needs it. I null-check lists because they start null.

terminology.plain: An ordered row of slots you can address by index.
terminology.precise: Ordered collection distinguished by indices. May nest collections (seven inner levels). Starts null until assigned.
terminology.example: List<Id> labIds = new List<Id>{ id1, id2 };
terminology.non_example: A related-list on a Lightning page is UI, not a List<T>.
terminology.boundary: Trigger.new is a list-like context variable; trigger frameworks are later.

terminology.plain: A bag of unique values with no promised order.
terminology.precise: Unordered collection that does not contain duplicates. Useful for Id deduplication before SOQL IN binds.
terminology.non_example: A permission set is a security artifact, not Set<T>.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: List: may contain duplicates and is ordered.
terminology.boundary: Do not invent sObject field-equality rules here; prefer Set<Id>.

terminology.plain: A wall of cubbies: one key opens one value.
terminology.precise: Unique keys each map to a single value. The bulk pattern is Map<Id, sObject> after one query.
terminology.example: Map<Id, Account> labById = new Map<Id, Account>([SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Id IN :ids]);
terminology.non_example: A Salesforce map/location field is geography, not Map<K,V>.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Set of keys versus the map itself.
terminology.boundary: Decimal keys with different scales can be unequal; see primitives caution.

terminology.plain: A walker that asks whether another item exists, then takes it.
terminology.precise: Iterator.hasNext() and next(); methods must be public or global. Iterable.iterator() supplies the walker. Used in custom traversals and some Batchable start methods.
terminology.non_example: A SOQL query locator is related but is not a hand-written Iterator class unless you wrap it.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: for-each: uses iteration without you implementing the interface.

terminology.plain: A typed container: list, set, or map.
terminology.precise: The Collections page names those three. You must specify type parameters. No documented item-count cap; heap applies.
terminology.non_example: A custom metadata 'collection' of records is data, not this type.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Array notation: syntactic sugar on a one-dimensional list.
terminology.boundary: Heap numbers live on the governors page.

terminology.plain: The everyday loop that walks a list or set.
terminology.precise: for (variable : array_or_set) from the Loops page. Prefer this over a manual iterator for in-memory collections.
terminology.non_example: A Flow Loop element is not Apex for-each.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: SOQL-for loop: walks a query, still a loop form from PROG-002.
terminology.boundary: Do not query inside this loop over Trigger.new.

terminology.plain: How much memory the transaction may hold, including collections.
terminology.precise: The Collections page: no item-count limit; general heap-size limit. Exact megabytes are on Execution Governors—do not invent them here.
terminology.example: A huge List<String> of payloads fails on heap, not on 'item 201'.
terminology.non_example: The 200-record trigger batch size is not a List capacity.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: SOQL 50,000 row limit: query rows, not collection capacity.
terminology.boundary: Cite governors if asked for a number (APEX-007).

terminology.plain: The set of keys living in a map.
terminology.precise: Map.keySet() yields a Set of keys you can iterate. Values are retrieved with get.
terminology.example: for (Id i : labById.keySet()) { Account a = labById.get(i); }
terminology.non_example: A Set you built separately is not automatically the map's keySet.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: values(): the collection of values, which may contain duplicates.
terminology.boundary: Method catalog is the Map class reference.

When an interview asks how iterators walk a collection versus a simple for-each.
When someone claims a collection can hold only 200 items and you need the heap correction.
When designing the Set-of-Ids then Map-by-Id pattern so a loop does not query.

Do not treat list/set/map choice as a governor-number memorization drill (APEX-007).
Do not implement a custom iterator when for-each over a list already walks the data.
Do not store secrets or real customer payloads in lab collections or debug dumps.

worked_example.scenario: A sandbox method receives two List<Id> of LAB_ Account Ids that overlap. It must produce unique Ids, query those Accounts once, and let a Case loop find Account.Name by AccountId without a second query per Case. Order of first-seen Ids must be kept for a debug string. No production data.
inputs: List<Id> from query A and query B

decisions.decision: Walk both Id lists into a List for first-seen order and a Set to skip duplicates.
decisions.because: List keeps order; Set enforces uniqueness.
decisions.rejected: Only a Set, which drops first-seen order

decisions.decision: Map<Id, Account> from one SOQL WHERE Id IN :uniqueIds.
decisions.because: Map is the key-to-value collection for lookup in the Case loop.
decisions.rejected: for (Case c : cases) { Account a = [SELECT Name FROM Account WHERE Id = :c.AccountId]; }

decisions.decision: Iterate Cases with for-each and map.get; no custom Iterator.
decisions.rejected: Hand-written Iterator for a simple list

configuration_or_code: Set<Id> seen = new Set<Id>(); List<Id> ordered = new List<Id>(); for (Id i : listA) { if (seen.add(i)) { ordered.add(i); } } same for listB;
Map<Id, Account> byId = new Map<Id, Account>([SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Id IN :seen]);
for (Case c : labCases) { Account a = byId.get(c.AccountId); }
worked_example.output: Unique Ids, stable first-seen order, one query, Case loop uses the map.
verification: seen.size() is less than listA.size()+listB.size() when overlaps exist.
No SOQL appears inside the Case loop.
worked_example.self_explanation: Set for uniqueness, list for order, map for lookup, for-each to walk.

hands_on_lab.environment: Disposable sandbox; synthetic LAB_ Accounts and Cases only.
starting_state_checks: Can insert LAB-named test records or use mocks in tests.
steps: In LAB_CollectionLab, build overlapping Id lists, a Set for unique Ids, and a List that records first-seen order.
Query once into Map<Id, Account> and walk a Case list with get.
Assert a duplicate Id appears once in the set and that the Case loop performs no extra query (single SOQL in the debug log / Limits.getQueries).
Write a tiny Iterator<Integer> for 1..3 with hasNext/next and consume it in a while loop; then delete it if unused.
guided_completion: If getQueries rose inside the Case loop, you still queried per row.
If the list allowed duplicate Ids in the 'unique' structure, you used a List where a Set belonged.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Explain in a comment why you would not tell an interviewer that a List maxes out at 200 elements.
evidence: Test asserting set size and map lookup.
Comment or assertion citing heap—not item cap—from the Collections page.
stop_recovery_cleanup: Delete LAB_ classes and synthetic rows.

decision_table.signal: UI or DML must keep insertion order, and duplicates are allowed or already unique.
decision_table.not: A Set if you still need stable first-seen order.
decision_table.why: A list is ordered and index-addressable; a set is unordered.

decision_table.signal: You must drop duplicate Ids before a SOQL IN clause.
decision_table.not: A List that you scan with nested loops to fake uniqueness.
decision_table.why: A set does not contain duplicates.

decision_table.signal: Inside a record loop you need a related row by Id.
decision_table.choose: Map<Id, sObject> filled by one query, then get.
decision_table.why: A map is the key-to-value collection; query-in-loop is the bulk fail.

decision_table.signal: Batchable start or an external sequence is not a simple in-memory list.
decision_table.choose: Implement Iterator/Iterable with hasNext and next.
decision_table.not: A custom iterator for a list you already have in memory.
decision_table.why: Custom Iterators are for custom traversal; for-each already walks lists and sets.

limitations: Does not quote heap megabytes; see governors.
Does not fully specify Set<sObject> equality.
Does not teach relationship SOQL instead of maps.
Iterator in Batchable start is a pointer, not a job-type lesson.
security_notes: Collections in debug logs can leak personal data.
Map keys that are Ids are still subject to sharing when you query.
Do not stash secrets in static maps.
common_mistakes: Querying inside a loop instead of Map.get.
Using a Set when order matters.
Calling add on a null List.
Writing Iterator for a trivial list walk.

interview_questions.question: How do you choose among lists, sets, maps, and iterators in Apex?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: List for order and index, set for uniqueness, map for key lookup, for-each to walk, custom Iterator only for special traversal. Heap, not a 200-item cap.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I start from the access pattern. If I need duplicates or positions, List. If I need unique Ids, Set. If I need get-by-Id in a loop, Map after one query. I iterate with for-each unless Batchable start or external paging needs Iterator. I correct anyone who says lists stop at 200 items. I initialize collections because they start null.
interview_questions.example: Set<Id> then Map<Id, Account> before a Case loop uses get.
tradeoffs: Set loses order vs list plus set
follow_ups: What is heap versus SOQL rows?
How do you iterate a map?

interview_questions.question: Why is Map<Id, sObject> the default bulk answer?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: A map is key to value. One query fills it; the record loop uses get instead of SOQL per row.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: The collection type matches the problem: lookup by Id. A list would force a scan. A set of Ids is the input to the query. Together they replace query-in-loop. I still mention heap if the map is enormous. I do not claim maps ignore sharing. I keep this distinct from relationship subqueries, which can also remove a loop query.
interview_questions.example: new Map<Id, Account>([SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Id IN :ids]).
tradeoffs: Heap of fat sObjects vs query fewer fields
follow_ups: What if the key is not Id?
Map constructor from a query list?
weak_answer_warnings: Using a list and nested loops to find Ids

interview_questions.question: Two lists of Ids overlap; UI must show first-seen order. Design the collections.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Walk both lists; Set.add tells you if new; if new, also push onto an ordered List. Query from the set.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Set alone drops order. List alone keeps duplicates. The pair is the usual answer: membership test plus ordered output. Then Map if I need records. I iterate with for-each. I do not sort the set and hope. I initialize both collections before add.
interview_questions.example: if (seen.add(id)) { ordered.add(id); } from the worked example.
follow_ups: Does Set.add return Boolean in Apex?
When would you sort the list after?
weak_answer_warnings: Only a set, then claiming it is ordered

interview_questions.question: When would you implement Iterator instead of using a list for-each?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: When traversal is custom, data is outside a simple list, or Batchable start returns Iterable.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: The Custom Iterators page is for instructions you cannot express as a list walk, including some Batchable start methods. hasNext/next must be public or global. For Trigger.new or a queried list, for-each is enough. I would not write Iterator as ceremony. I separate this from choosing Queueable versus Batch.
interview_questions.example: CustomIterator implementing Iterator<Account> as in the Developer Guide sample shape.

interview_questions.question: A teammate says the list cannot exceed 200 elements so they chunk by hand. Response?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: The Collections page says no item-count cap; heap is the limit. 200 is a different platform batch size.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I ask what they are chunking for. Trigger batch size 200 and for-loop list batch size 200 are neighboring facts on the governors page, not List capacity. If they hit heap, they should query fewer fields or process in platform batches. If they hit SOQL rows, that is a query limit. I will not let a design review invent a 200-item List type limit.
interview_questions.example: A List of 500 Ids is legal; a 200-row trigger invocation is a different boundary.
tradeoffs: Heap vs row limits vs trigger batch
follow_ups: When is Batch Apex the right chunker?

interview_questions.question: map.get returns null in the loop even though you queried. Checks?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Wrong key, query did not include that Id, or you built Map<String, ...> with 15-char versus 18-char mismatch.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I print keySet versus the lookup Id. I confirm the SOQL WHERE Id IN :ids used the same set. I check I did not store Name as the key. Id 15-to-18 conversion is a primitives topic; I mention it as Needs verification if the keys look truncated. I also check the map was assigned, not left null.
interview_questions.example: byId.get(c.AccountId) is null when AccountId was not in the queried set.
weak_answer_warnings: Querying again inside the loop as the fix

interview_questions.question: When would you avoid a Map and use a relationship query instead?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: When a single SOQL can walk parent or child fields and you do not need an independent Id lookup later.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Collections are not a mandate to query twice. If Case.Account.Name is available through a relationship query, I may skip the map. I use a map when I already have mixed sources of Ids or I will look up from several loops. This lesson still teaches the map because interviewers ask for it. I do not invent relationship syntax here beyond that decision.
interview_questions.example: SELECT Id, Account.Name FROM Case versus Map of Account.
tradeoffs: One fatter query vs a map from a second query
follow_ups: When do relationship queries hit other limits?
Can a map still help after a relationship query?

interview_questions.question: Teach list, set, map, and iterator with the parcel hub and where it breaks.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Numbered conveyor is list, unique scanner is set, cubby wall is map, night walker is iterator. It breaks because sets are unordered and 200 is not a hub capacity.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I walk a parcel through slots, the unique scan, and a barcode cubby. I have the walker ask hasNext. I then say a physical tray looks ordered even when a Set is not, sObject equality is not a barcode, and people keep citing 200 parcels because they remember trigger batch size. I finish with Set plus Map Apex, not a drawing only.
interview_questions.example: seen.add(id) plus byId.get(id) narrated as scan then cubby.
tradeoffs: Analogy vs writing the three declarations
